# DsNA(Digital sigNature for Audios): A Unique Method to Fingerprint Audio Files Generated by Text to Speech

[PDF](https://www.isca-archive.org/interspeech_2026/gourav26_interspeech.pdf) · [ISCA page](https://www.isca-archive.org/interspeech_2026/gourav26_interspeech.html)

**TL;DR** — DsNA is a lightweight post-generation framework that embeds cryptographic digital signatures into text-to-speech audio by interleaving signature shards with audio chunks, preserving an SNR of 45.2 dB.

## Problem

The increasing realism of neural text-to-speech systems creates serious concerns regarding audio provenance, authenticity, and malicious misuse. Traditional audio fingerprinting relies on external lookup databases or content matching rather than embedding verifiable provenance directly into the generated file. This creates a gap in achieving self-contained, self-verifiable synthetic speech artifacts.

## Method

The DsNA framework acts as a post-generation layer that processes synthesized .wav audio files alongside associated metadata without modifying the underlying TTS architecture. An audio chunker splits the waveform into two equal chunks, while a fingerprint generator creates a compact digital signature using RSA-inspired cryptographic hashing. A shard generator splits this digital signature into three shards, which are then interleaved directly with the audio chunks to form the final signed output. A reverse verification pipeline can subsequently unpack these interleaved shards to authenticate the audio.

## Results

Evaluated on 250 samples generated from a TTS model, the framework achieved an identical signal-to-noise ratio of 45.2 dB for both original and fingerprinted audio. Perceptual and linguistic evaluations showed negligible impact, with MOS dropping only slightly from 4.51 to 4.48, while Character Error Rate (CER) and Word Error Rate (WER) remained constant at 1.8% and 2.6% respectively.

## Code

None released (as of this page's `updated` date). If you are an author with a repo, please claim this entry — see CONTRIBUTING.md.

## Applications

Developers and platforms deploying text-to-speech synthesis can use this framework for watermarking and verifying synthetic audio provenance to prevent deepfake misuse.

## Limitations

The current study serves as an initial proof of concept and leaves open the evaluation of perceptual quality under broader conditions, robustness to real-world transformations like compression and noise, and resilience against adversarial manipulation.
